question.text: What is a 'short strangle' strategy and what are its risks?

answer.text: Sell an OTM call and sell an OTM put — profits from time decay in rangebound markets. Max profit = total premium received. Risk: unlimited on the upside (short call) and substantial on the downside (short put)
Buy an OTM call and buy an OTM put for directional exposure
Sell an ATM call and sell an ATM put (this would be a short straddle)
A risk-free strategy that guarantees premium income

explanation.text: The Logic: Short strangle: receive premium from selling both OTM call and OTM put. Profit if underlying stays between the two strikes. Max profit = total premium received. Loss is large/unlimited above the call strike and substantial below the put strike. Requires significant margin. The Trap: Buying both is a LONG strangle (different payoff). Selling ATM is a short straddle (narrower profit range). Short strangles are definitely NOT risk-free — they have potentially unlimited losses if the underlying moves outside the strike range. Note: The short strangle appears in both Equity Derivatives (Series VIII) and Currency Derivatives (Series I) workbooks as a neutral, premium-receiving strategy. The mechanics — capped premium income against unlimited/substantial loss outside the strike range — are identical across asset classes.
